opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of those things that sounds like boring housekeeping but actually matters a lot for whether we can trust any of the numbers we report.

The basic issue is that these models are trained on enormous web-scale corpora, and benchmarks live on the web too. The test questions, the answers, sometimes whole GitHub repos with the evaluation sets. So if you're not careful, the model may have literally seen the test during pretraining. Then when it does well, you can't tell whether it learned the underlying skill or just memorized that particular question. Those are very different things, and the whole point of a benchmark is to measure the first one.

It's gotten more pressing as datasets grow and become less transparent. With smaller, curated datasets you could reason about what was in there. Now people train on trillions of tokens, often without releasing the data, so outside researchers can't even check. That's part of why I care about open data and documenting what goes into training. If the data is open, the community can run n-gram overlap checks or more semantic matching and say, "this benchmark is likely contaminated for this model, take that result with a grain of salt."

There are also subtler versions. It's not only exact copies. It can be paraphrases, translations, or the same problem with different numbers. Exact-match filtering misses those, so decontamination is really a spectrum of how aggressive you want to be and how much risk you'll tolerate.

And it matters beyond leaderboards. If we overestimate capabilities because of contamination, we make bad research decisions: we think a method works when it doesn't, or that a model generalizes to a domain it hasn't really mastered. So for me, decontamination, along with things like held-out or freshly created evaluations, is part of doing science properly with these models rather than just chasing numbers.

r001.rationale: The response says a model may have seen the test during pretraining, making it unclear whether strong results show learned skill or memorization rather than generalization.

r002.rationale: It notes that training corpora contain trillions of tokens and are difficult for outsiders to check, but does not identify the computational expense of checking evaluation samples against them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think decontamination is important for a pretty simple reason: these models are trained on a huge chunk of the internet, and the benchmarks we use to evaluate them are also on the internet. So if you don't do anything about it, there's a real chance the model has literally seen the test questions, maybe even with the answers, during pretraining. And then when you measure its performance, you're not measuring whether it can reason or generalize, you're partly measuring whether it memorized the test set.

That matters because the whole point of a benchmark is to be a proxy for how the model will do on things it hasn't seen. If the score is inflated by contamination, you can draw the wrong conclusions, like thinking one model is much better than another when really it just had more of the benchmark leak into its training data. And it compounds over time, because popular benchmarks get discussed, copied, reformatted, put into GitHub repos, and so they end up in more and more crawls. Older or very well-known benchmarks are especially at risk.

What we try to do, for example in work like OLMo or in the data work I've been involved in, is actually look for overlap between the training data and the evaluation sets, usually with n-gram matching or some fuzzier version of that, and either remove those documents or at least report how much overlap there is. It's not perfect, because paraphrases and translations can slip through, and there's a question of what threshold counts as contamination. But being transparent about it is a big part of it. If you release your training data, other people can check for themselves, which is one of the reasons I care a lot about open data.

And I'd say the bigger picture is that it's really about trust in the numbers. If we want to make progress as a field and compare models honestly, we need to be confident that a gain on a benchmark reflects actual capability, not leakage. Decontamination is one of the basic hygiene steps for that.

r001.rationale: Explains that models may have seen benchmark questions and answers during pretraining, causing scores to reflect memorization rather than reasoning or generalization.

r002.rationale: Does not identify checking evaluation samples against pretraining corpora containing trillions of tokens as computationally expensive.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that we want to measure how well a model generalizes to something it hasn’t seen before. If the evaluation questions—or their answers—are already in the training data, then a high score could reflect memorization rather than the capability we’re trying to measure.

And that’s particularly tricky with large language models because we train them on so much data from the internet. Benchmarks are often publicly available, so they can end up in that training corpus, even unintentionally. Decontamination is about identifying and removing that overlap so we can have more confidence in the evaluation.

It also matters for comparing models. If one model has seen a benchmark during training and another hasn’t, their scores aren’t really measuring the same thing. And it’s not enough to just check for exact matches, because a question might appear in a slightly different form. So decontamination is challenging, but it’s an important part of making benchmark results meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation overlap can make a high score reflect memorization rather than the ability to generalize to unseen material.

r002.rationale: It notes that models train on a large amount of internet data and that decontamination is challenging, but does not identify checking against trillions of pretraining tokens as computationally expensive.

sol-6.1.text:
The main concern is that you want to measure how well a model generalizes to new problems. If the evaluation examples are already in its training data, it might get a high score because it has memorized those examples, rather than because it can actually solve the task.

And this is particularly tricky with large language models because we train on so much of the internet, where a lot of these benchmarks are publicly available. So data decontamination means checking for overlap and removing benchmark examples from the training data. It’s not a perfect process—examples can be paraphrased or appear in different forms—but it helps make the evaluation more trustworthy and comparisons between models more meaningful.

r001.rationale: It says overlap with training data can yield a high score through memorization rather than genuine generalization.

r002.rationale: It mentions training on much of the internet and checking for overlap, but does not identify trillion-token pretraining corpora or the computational expense of checking them.
